messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor-node load $R_L$ from a piezoelectric transducer.
    *   Operating conditions: S1-S6 (varying $I_p, f, C_p, R_L, T$).
    *   Constraints:
        *   $v_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$ (settled mean output)
        *   $v_{max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$ (absolute maximum)
        *   $v_{pp} \le 0.05\text{ V}$ (ripple)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$ (startup time)
        *   $dv \le 0.02\text{ V}$ (stability)
    *   Piezo Model: Sinusoidal current source $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ and $20\text{ M}\Omega$.
    *   Reference Design (FBR): Full-bridge rectifier.
        *   S2 FAIL ($v_{avg} < 1.8\text{V}$ - too much load)
        *   S3 FAIL ($v_{max} > 3.6\text{V}$ - overvoltage, $v_{pp} > 0.05\text{V}$)
        *   S4 FAIL ($v_{avg} < 1.8\text{V}$ - weak excitation)
        *   S5 FAIL ($dv > 0.02\text{V}$ - instability/drift)
    *   Key Observations:
        *   The open-circuit voltage is low ($\sim 3.2\text{ V}$), so diode drops (even Schottky $\sim 0.25\text{V}$) are significant.
        *   Standard FBR loses $2 \times 0.25\text{V} = 0.5\text{V}$.
        *   We need a way to increase efficiency (lower the voltage drop) and regulate the output voltage (prevent overvoltage in S3).

    *   *Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI):* Uses an inductor and switches to invert the voltage on $C_p$ at the peaks, significantly increasing extracted energy. This addresses S2 and S4 (low power/high load).
    *   *Voltage Regulation:* A Zener clamp (DZ33) can prevent $v_{max}$ from exceeding $3.6\text{V}$.
    *   *Storage:* A capacitor on the output is essential for ripple and stability.

    *   **Topology 1: SSHI with Full-Bridge (Active Rectification/Inversion)**
        *   SSHI typically uses a switch and inductor to flip the charge of $C_p$.
        *   Circuit: Piezo $\to$ SSHI inversion $\to$ Full Bridge $\to$ Output Capacitor.
        *   Simplified SSHI: Inductor $L$ and switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo (or part of the path) that closes at peaks.
        *   Better yet, a "Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction" (SECE) or a simple SSHI implementation.
        *   Actually, the simplest SSHI is: Inductor $L$ and Switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo. When $S$ closes, $C_p$ resonates with $L$, flipping the voltage. Then a rectifier collects the energy.

    *   **Topology 2: Synchronous Rectification / Buck-Boost (too complex for 16 components?)**
        *   Let's stick to SSHI + Bridge + Clamp.

    *   **Topology 3: Parallel SSHI / SECE variant**
        *   Instead of a full bridge, maybe a half-bridge or a specific SSHI structure.
        *   Let's try an "Inductive-SSHI" where the inductor is used to flip the voltage, followed by a diode bridge to the output.

    *   *SSHI structure:*
        1.  Piezo (pzp, pzn).
        2.  Inductor $L$ and Switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo? No, usually the switch and inductor are in series, and the combination is in parallel with the piezo.
        3.  Let's refine:
            *   Piezo terminals: `pzp`, `pzn`.
            *   Inductor $L1$ between `pzp` and `n1`.
            *   Switch $S1$ between `n1` and `pzn`.
            *   Controller $G1$: `edges: both`, `ton` calculated as $\pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.
            *   This flips the voltage on $C_p$.
            *   Now we need to get that energy to `out`. A full-bridge rectifier (4x DSCH) connected to `pzp` and `pzn` will charge the `out` capacitor.

    *   *Check constraints:*
        *   S3 (Overvoltage): Add a Zener diode `DZ33` from `out` to `0`.
        *   S2/S4 (Low Power): SSHI increases power by flipping the piezo voltage, effectively reducing the "internal" impedance and increasing the voltage swing.

    *   *Component count check (Topology 1):*
        - L1 (1)
        - S1 (1)
        - G1 (1)
        - D1-D4 (4)
        - C_out (1)
        - DZ1 (1)
        - Total: 9 components (well within 16).

    *   *Let's consider an alternative to the Full Bridge:*
        Maybe a half-bridge if $pzn$ is grounded? The problem states $pzp$ and $pzn$ are the piezo terminals. Usually, one is tied to ground if it's a single-ended source, but the model provides both. The reference design used a full bridge. Let's keep the full bridge for robustness.

    *   *Wait, let's refine the SSHI placement:*
        The standard SSHI: The inductor and switch are in parallel with the piezo. The rectifier is then placed across the piezo.
        - Piezo: pzp, pzn.
        - $L1$ from pzp to n1.
        - $S1$ from n1 to pzn.
        - $G1$ (SYNC) closes $S1$ at peaks.
        - Rectifier: $D1$(pzp, out), $D2$(pzn, out), $D3$(0, pzp), $D4$(0, pzn).
        - Storage: $C_{out}$ from out to 0.
        - Clamp: $DZ1$ from out to 0.

    *   *Is there a more efficient way?*
        The diode bridge still has a 0.5V drop. For very low voltage sources, this is a killer. However, the piezo open-circuit voltage is $\sim 3.2\text{V}$. SSHI increases the effective voltage.

    *   *Alternative: SECE (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction)*
        SECE uses an inductor and a switch to move the charge from $C_p$ to $C_{out}$ almost regardless of the voltage on $C_{out}$, as long as the peak voltage is higher.
        - $L$ from `pzp` to `n1`.
        - $S1$ from `n1` to `out`.
        - This is essentially a buck-converter-like transfer.
        - But SSHI is more standard for this specific task.

    *   Let's propose a few variations.

    *   **Design 1: SSHI + Full Bridge + Zener** (The classic improvement)
    *   **Design 2: SECE-like (Direct Transfer)**
        - Inductor $L$ and Switch $S$ transferring charge directly to `out`.
        - This avoids the full bridge drop.
        - Components: $L1$(pzp, n1), $S1$(n1, out), $G1$(SYNC), $C_{out}$(out, 0), $DZ1$(out, 0).
        - Wait, SECE needs to handle both polarities. So two switches or a bridge.
        - Two switches: $S1$(n1, out) and $S2$(n2, out) with $L1$(pzp, n1) and $L2$(pzn, n2). This might be too many components.

    *   **Design 3: SSHI with a simplified rectifier (Half Bridge if one terminal is ground)**
        - The test bench allows us to treat `pzn` as ground? No, "The piezo model between pzp and pzn". It's a floating source. A full bridge is safer.

    *   Let's go with a very optimized SSHI + Full Bridge + Zener for Proposal 1.
    *   For Proposal 2, let's try a simpler SSHI using a "half-bridge" approach if we assume `pzn` is ground, but to be safe, I'll use a full bridge. Actually, let's try a different inductor-switch configuration.

    *   *Wait, look at the Reference Design again:*
        FBR: S1(ok), S2(FAIL vavg), S3(FAIL vmax), S4(FAIL vavg), S5(FAIL dv), S6(ok).
        - S2 and S4 fail on voltage. SSHI will help.
        - S3 fails on max voltage. Zener will help.
        - S5 fails on $dv$ (stability). This is often due to the $C_{out}$ value or the power balance. A larger $C_{out}$ or better extraction helps.

    *   *Proposal 1: SSHI-FBR (Full Bridge)*
        - $L1$: 10mH, $S1$ (SYNC, both edges), Rectifier (4x DSCH), $C_{out}$, $DZ33$.
    *   *Proposal 2: SSHI-HB (Half Bridge)*
        - If we connect `pzn` to `0`, we can use a half-bridge. But the prompt says the piezo is between `pzp` and `pzn`. If I connect `pzn` to `0` via a resistor or directly, it's a half-bridge. But the most general way is the full bridge. Let's try a "Parallel-SSHI" where the inductor-switch is in parallel with the piezo and we use a bridge.

    *   *Proposal 3: a different synchronous approach (SECE)*
        - SECE: $L1$(pzp, n1), $S1$(n1, out), $L2$(pzn, n2), $S2$(n2, out). This transfers charge from both peaks directly to the output.
        - $G1$: edges: pos, $G2$: edges: neg.
        - This avoids the 0.5V diode drop entirely! This should significantly help S2 and S4.
        - Components: $L1, L2, S1, S2, G1, G2, C_{out}, DZ1$. (8 components).

    *   S2 and S4 are the hardest (low $v_{avg}$).
    *   Diode drops are the main enemy.
    *   SECE (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction) is superior because it's a switch-based transfer, not diode-based.

    *   *SECE Design:*
        - `L1` between `pzp` and `n1`.
        - `S1` between `n1` and `out`.
        - `L2` between `pzn` and `n2`.
        - `S2` between `n2` and `out`.
        - `G1` (SYNC): `edges: "pos"`, `ton` small.
        - `G2` (SYNC): `edges: "neg"`, `ton` small.
        - `Cout` (out, 0).
        - `DZ1` (out, 0) for clamping.

    *   *Wait, the SYNC controller is limited to 2.*
        G1 and G2 are 2 controllers. Perfect.

    *   *Let's double check SECE logic:*
        At the positive peak of $V_{pzp}$, $S1$ closes, $L1$ transfers charge from $C_p$ to $C_{out}$.
        At the negative peak of $V_{pzp}$ (positive peak of $V_{pzn}$), $S2$ closes, $L2$ transfers charge from $C_p$ to $C_{out}$.
        This is very efficient.

    *   *Wait, one more thing:*
        In SECE, the inductor is usually connected from the piezo to the switch.
        - Piezo: `pzp` $\to$ `L1` $\to$ `S1` $\to$ `out`.
        - Piezo: `pzn` $\to$ `L2` $\to$ `S2` $\to$ `out`.
        Yes, this works.

    *   *What about the "settled" ($dv$) and "ripple" ($v_{pp}$) requirements?*
        A large $C_{out}$ will handle $v_{pp}$. $dv$ is about power balance. SECE is very efficient, so it should settle well.

    *   *Wait, let me refine Proposal 1 as well:*
        Just in case SECE is too aggressive, SSHI + Full Bridge is a safer bet for some conditions.

    *   *Let's refine the components for Proposal 1 (SSHI + FBR):*
        - $L1$: `pzp` to `n1`
        - $S1$: `n1` to `pzn`
        - $G1$: `edges: both`
        - $D1$: `pzp` to `out`
        - $D2$: `pzn` to `out`
        - $D3$: `0` to `pzp`
        - $D4$: `0` to `pzn`
        - $C_{out}$: `out` to `0`
        - $DZ1$: `out` to `0` (Zener)

    *   *Refining Proposal 2 (SECE):*
        - $L1$: `pzp` to `n1`
        - $S1$: `n1` to `out`
        - $L2$: `pzn` to `n2`
        - $S2$: `n2` to `out`
        - $G1$: `edges: pos`
        - $G2$: `edges: neg`
        - $C_{out}$: `out` to `0`
        - $DZ1$: `out` to `0` (Zener)

    *   *Comparing Proposal 1 and 2:*
        Proposal 2 (SECE) is far more likely to hit $v_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{V}$ for S2 and S4 because it doesn't have the diode bridge drop.

    *   *Wait, is there a Proposal 3?*
        Maybe a "Half-Bridge SECE" where we tie `pzn` to `0`?
        If `pzn` is tied to `0`, we only need one inductor and one switch for the positive peak. But we lose the negative peak unless we have another inductor. So SECE is better.

    *   Let's try a third one: "SSHI with active rectification" (using switches instead of diodes in the bridge). But that requires more than 2 SYNC controllers (we need 4 for a bridge).

    *   Let's stick to:
        1. SSHI-FBR (Safe, but diode drops)
        2. SECE (High efficiency, switch-based)
        3. a variation of SECE or a different inductor-based circuit.
        Actually, a "Synchronous Charge Extraction" using a single inductor and a switch might work if the piezo is biased. But let's keep it simple.

    *   *One detail on SECE:*
        The $L$ value needs to be chosen carefully to avoid too much ripple or overshooting. But the evolutionary tuner handles values. I just need the connectivity.
        The $ton$ for SECE is also small.

    *   *Let's refine Proposal 2's components for the JSON:*
        - $L1$: `pzp` to `n1`, value 10mH
        - $S1$: `n1` to `out`, ctrl: `G1`
        - $L2$: `pzn` to `n2`, value 10mH
        - $S2$: `n2` to `out`, ctrl: `G2`
        - $G1$: SYNC, edges: "pos", ton: 1e-4
        - $G2$: SYNC, edges: "neg", ton: 1e-4
        - $C1$: `out` to `0`, value 2.2uF
        - $DZ1$: `out` to `0`, model: "DZ33"

    *   *Wait, let me double-check the DZ33 orientation:*
        "Zener clamp on out: ['0', 'out'] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at 3.3 V)."
        Okay, so `["0", "out"]`.

    *   *Final check on Component Count:*
        - SSHI-FBR: L1, S1, G1, D1, D2, D3, D4, C1, DZ1 = 9.
        - SECE: L1, S1, L2, S2, G1, G2, C1, DZ1 = 8.

    *   *Wait, the Reference Design FBR used 2.2uF.* Let's use similar values for the starting point.

    *   *One more thing for SECE:*
        Does SECE need a diode to prevent the storage cap from discharging back into the piezo?
        Actually, the inductor $L$ and the switch $S$ act as a one-way transfer during $ton$. When the switch is open, there's no path. The only path back would be through the inductor during the $ton$ phase, but the $L$ is designed to transfer charge from $C_p$ to $C_{out}$ because $V_{pzp}$ is at its peak.
        Wait, in a real SECE, you often have a diode to prevent reverse flow. Let's add one just in case.
        $L1 \to S1 \to D1 \to$ out.
        But $S1$ is a switch. If $S1$ is off, no current flows. If $S1$ is on, $L1$ conducts.
        Let's see... if $V_{out} > V_{pzp}$, when $S1$ closes, current would flow from $out$ to $pzp$.
        To prevent this, a diode $D1$ between $S1$ and `out` would be helpful.
        So: `L1` $\to$ `n1`, `S1` $\to$ `n1` to `n3`, `D1` $\to$ `n3` to `out`.
        Actually, $L1$ and $S1$ are used to transfer charge. The diode is usually placed *before* the inductor or *after* the switch. Let's put a Schottky diode `D1` between $S1$ and `out` to ensure the current only goes *to* the capacitor.

    *   *Revised SECE:*
        - `L1` (pzp, n1)
        - `S1` (n1, n3), ctrl: `G1`
        - `D1` (n3, out), model: "DSCH"
        - `L2` (pzn, n2)
        - `S2` (n2, n4), ctrl: `G2`
        - `D2` (n4, out), model: "DSCH"
        - `G1` (SYNC, pos)
        - `G2` (SYNC, neg)
        - `C1` (out, 0)
        - `DZ1` (0, out)
        - Total: 10 components.

    *   *Let's think about the "settled" and "startup" requirements:*
        Startup $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$. SECE is very fast.
        Settled $dv \le 0.02\text{V}$. $C_{out}$ and the efficiency of SECE should make it stable.

    *   *One last check on SSHI-FBR:*
        The diode bridge is simple. The SSHI part flips the piezo voltage, effectively doubling the voltage seen by the bridge.
        `L1` (pzp, n1)
        `S1` (n1, pzn), ctrl: `G1`
        `G1` (SYNC, both)
        `D1-D4` (Full Bridge)
        `C1` (out, 0)
        `DZ1` (0, out)
        This is also a strong candidate.

    *   *Let's provide these two.*

    *   *Refining Proposal 1 (SSHI-FBR):*
        `L1` [pzp, n1], `S1` [n1, pzn], `G1` [SYNC, both], `D1` [pzp, out], `D2` [pzn, out], `D3` [0, pzp], `D4` [0, pzn], `C1` [out, 0], `DZ1` [0, out].

    *   *Refining Proposal 2 (SECE):*
        `L1` [pzp, n1], `S1` [n1, n3], `D1` [n3, out], `L2` [pzn, n2], `S2` [n2, n4], `D2` [n4, out], `G1` [SYNC, pos], `G2` [SYNC, neg], `C1` [out, 0], `DZ1` [0, out].

    *   *Wait, I can propose 3. Let's try a "SSHI-Half-Bridge" for the 3rd:*
        Connect `pzn` to `0` through a resistor (though the test bench already adds 1GOhm).
        Then use only one half of the bridge.
        `L1` [pzp, n1], `S1` [n1, pzn], `G1` [SYNC, both], `D1` [pzp, out], `D2` [0, pzp], `C1` [out, 0], `DZ1` [0, out].
        This is just a variation of Proposal 1. Let's try something else.
        What if we use a "charge pump" style? No, that's too complex.
        Let's just stick to Proposal 1 and 2. They are the most robust strategies.

    *   Actually, I'll add a third: A "Simplified SECE" without the diodes, just to see if the tuner can handle it.
        `L1` [pzp, n1], `S1` [n1, out], `L2` [pzn, n2], `S2` [n2, out], `G1` [SYNC, pos], `G2` [SYNC, neg], `C1` [out, 0], `DZ1` [0, out].

    *   Wait, one final check on the diode bridge for Proposal 1:
        D1: [pzp, out], D2: [pzn, out], D3: [0, pzp], D4: [0, pzn].
        Is this correct?
        If `pzp` is positive, $D1$ conducts $\to$ `out`. $D4$ is reverse, $D2$ is reverse, $D3$ is reverse.
        If `pzn` is positive, $D2$ conducts $\to$ `out`. $D1$ is reverse, $D3$ is reverse, $D4$ is reverse.
